Title: Five New Sabbat War Card texts

Messages.Author: ChickLewis
Messages.Body:
Here are the card texts of five cards from Sabbat War which I believe are new
in this release. I got them at the Pre-release event at Third Planet in
Southern California, which was really big fun. Please forgive me, but I’m
not conversant with the "official" way to do card data, so I hope this format
may suffice:

San Nicolas de los Servitas
Equipment Location
Requires Lasombra
Cost, Two blood
This equipment card represents a unique location and does not count as
equipment while in play. Actions directed at this Lasombra cost an additional
pool. If this location is burned, the Lasombra with this card takes two damage
(damage not preventable). This card cannot be contested. Any card that would
contest this location is immediately burned before contesting begins.

Eternal Vigilance
Action
(no symbols)
Cost, One blood
Requires a ready Archbishop, Priscus, or Cardinal. +1 stealth
Put this card on the acting vampire. During an action, the Sabbat vampire with
this card can pay a blood to untap and attempt to block. Burn this card if
this Sabbat vampire goes to torpor.

Oubliette
Combat strike
Requires Otenebration
Cost, One blood
inf: Strike, Combat ends
sup: As above, and the opposing minion burns one blood (or life) after combat.

Templar
Political action
(no symbols)
(no cost)
Political Card - Worth 1 Vote. Called by any Bishop, Archbishop, Priscus or
Cardinal at +1 stealth.
Choose a Sabbat vampire. Successful referendum makes the vampire a templar. A
templar may enter combat with a ready vampire controlled by another Methuslah
as a +1 stealth D action. Any Sabbat vampire may call a referendum to remove
this ability as a +1 stealth political action.

Waste Management Operation
Master
Requires Brujah Antitribu
Cost , one pool
Master: unique location. Tap during your discard phase to move a card from
your ash heap to the bottom of your library.

Why would it be? If you play a political deck you're not likely to have
it votes away through a Disputed Territory, so then they'll have to
take actions to burn the blood, which are more or less wasted actions.
Only problem would be Arson, but there's usually tons of other
locations that people rather consider to burn. The prey of a Meth using
Backways would for example like to get rid of that one (esp if the
Gangrel is playing with Dominate and the prey doesn't have that much
intercept) than to try burn my PB if I were his prey since I could pull
through my most critical votes even without my PB (because my deck is a
political one). If I don't have a vote deck thenthe PB can be used to
try disrupt votes directed against me, Disputed Territory included. If
I still don't succeed, he's at least wasted an action to take control
over my PB (an action he'd otherwise possibly use to take another of my
locations like Elder Library. Thanks to PB he now needs to first take
my PB or at least burn the vounters on it, in order to get the votes to
take my EL). In a worst acse scenario he wasted an action and a DT
(that he could have used for better purposes, since if he plays a
political deck any actions trying to uphold his vote lock are wasted
actions). If my PB helps him to get a vote lock then he could possibly
have achieved it anyway through other means, and it should also be hard
for him to pull through a DT when I have my PB to vote agaisnt it.

Also, every deck should have some stationary intercept cards to put
into play, and political decks usually can't pull out that much stealth
for an Arson. In conclusion, you can never be safe. But that applies to
every location, and IMO PB isn't powerful enough in *other* people's
view to have them try get rid of it asap, whilst the PB is deifnately
good enough to be included in most decks.

When I said location having an impact I used the word "really" to
emphasize that people don't bother to burn even good locations unless
it affects them so much that they lose the game if they don't burn it.
The PB could be such a card in *some* cases but in many other not,
since when it comes to votes people tend to think "I block the
political action instead when he tries to play it, instead of burning
the blood on the PB all the time", a thought that's not so dumb either.
Why waste actions trying to get rid of a card if you're not even sure
the card will have an impact on the game? (i.e. if I inlcude it in a
non-political deck, only a political deck would be interested in trying
to get rid of it, adn even then it's quite doubtful since they will
have BO's etc to help them get through their votes, PB or not).

Table management is obnoxiously difficult with a hyper-combat deck.
To make your combats 100% effective, you don't have room for intercept
or untap - at least not the effective variety, where you can actually
catch something other than the occasional +1 stealth action. The
vampires in question don't have the disciplines for bleed bounce or
vote defense, so your defenses MUST be subtracting any voters or
bleeders that take actions you don't like, with extreme prejudice.

Ideally, you beat up all of your prey's vampires as soon as they get
influenced out, before they ever get to take an action - and with your
spare vampires, you beat up any of your predator's vampires that look
threatening, but you leave his defenders alone (out of Ozmo, Roland
Bishop, and Zoe, you beat the crap out of Ozmo first, and then Roland
if he ever takes a bleed action. Zoe is not a significant offensive
threat without skill cards, so she can live until she bounces a bleed
- then she'll need to go too.)

Once you run out of vampires in your immediate vicinity that need to
die, you bleed your defenseless prey for 1 with each vampire. Do this
lots. As necessary, you will need to look around the table and see
who is building up to be too strong - is your grand-predator making
short work of your predator? That won't do. Go "adjust" one of his
vampires. Is your grandprey building up a huge pool gain monster with
the total lack of pressure? Go knock his Prince's block off so he'll
quit 5th Traditioning.

A lot of times, you'll win 3-1 or 4-1 - your predator will have been
ousted at some point, and there's not a lot you can do about it.
Someone who is bound and determined to hammer you with every vampire
they can is just going to have to lose those vampires, and if that
leaves them defenseless, bad cess to them.

The problems with the deck come in when Obedience and Fortitude make
an appearance. Obedience will wedge your hand horribly by making you
waste a Rush action and not letting you move any cards - possibly
leaving you Rushless. Fortitude is not AS bad, since you get to move
cards, press, and get to the next Rush action, and they will
eventually run out of Skin of Steel/Rolling with the Punches -
possibly that combat since IG provides a press. Superior Mettle at
superior is a real pain in the butt for POT/OBF decks - one card
basically walls up the entire combat and you MUST burn down your hand
in order to get to another Rush. POT/CEL decks ignore this, but since
they rely on the extra strikes, sometimes Skin of Steel can be nastier
- and the vamp selection for POT/OBF is much better. Especially with
Ox, who removes the need for Potence skill cards in such a deck, IMO -
think 2 Beast, 2 Ox, 2 Nigel, 2 Olivia, 2 Agatha, 1 Duck, 1 Koko.
Hasina and Lupo can make an appearance in place of an Ox and a Nigel,
but then you want a couple skill cards back again.

The other problems come in when other people have combat decks, and
now it's a question of who does their combat better. Close-range guys
you can normally handle, except for the Gangrel and other POT decks
(mutual annihilation! whee). Long-range guys can be trouble, as they
often pack enough maneuvers to guarantee their range against POT
decks.

maneuvers and Fortitude as their combat defense.]

> of sheer frustration. My combat decks come out, kill two to six vampires,
> and get ousted with 0 to 1 victory points. Do I just suck at table
> management, or is there some Deep Juju to playing combat I'm
> just totally oblivious to?

There is some fairly deep Juju. The key is putting enough pressure on
your predator so that they don't kill you. But not too much, because
then you get a new, really strong predator. You have to put pressure on
your prey (that's how you win) but not so much that you ignore your
predator. Very rarely, you will need to kill something across the table
(a) because it's threatening you or (b) because sometimes you need to
threaten people across the table to get them to help you, and sometimes
you need to follow up on your threats.

If your deck is constructed right, then at any time on your turn, you
should be able to point at a vampire and make it die by sheer force of
having a monster combat deck (will factors in there somewhere). The
tricky part is knowing who to kill. Sometimes, you bide your time,
especially when the table is where you want it. Know when to stop
killing everything and start bleeding. Have a long-term plan. Your
deck is going to run out of cards before anyone else's. What do you do
then? My decks tend to have a little pool gain, a little bleed bonus,
and a little strength increase. _All_ permanent. Having a vampire with
inherent +1 bleed (man, I love that Commander Sela) or having a random
Tasha Morgan in your deck can make the difference between winning and
not. Again, this must all be in moderation. The vast majority of your
deck must be concentrated on kill, kill, kill.

Note: If your group is wise to your combat-y ways, you may not be able
to win with your deck. In this case, the strategy becomes "punish them
for trying too hard". Make a deck against which all their Skins of
Steel, Majesty, and Obedience are completely wasted; a stealth-bleed
deck.

But if the card is so marginal that you don't care if your opponents can

> opponents slow down and work carefully as they're trying to screw
> with you. And unlike a bleed deck, if you wind up in combat with
> an opposing minion, that's generally a good thing, a step in the

My (considerable) experience with this kind of deck has shown me that
this is simply incorrect. First, the card(s) which provide intercept
take up slots in your deck, making your combat less effective. Second,
you have to waste an action or a master phase getting the intercept
out. Third, you then have to waste a minion _not_ rushing something to
sit around waiting to block something. And very often, this leads to
you beating up your predator instead of your prey, which is not always
what you want. The key to winning with a rush deck is not "beat up
everything you can". If my prey has a Ventrue deck with lots of
anti-combat and my predator has some feeb deck with weak vampires, it
might be tempting to vent my frustrations and obliterate all my
predator's vampires. But that will lose me the game.

conflicting lessons. There's all kinds of reasons for this: metagame,
talking about different kinds of rush combat decks, using larger vs.
smaller vampires, and personal strengths and weaknesses in play.

> First, the card(s) which provide intercept take up slots in your
> deck, making your combat less effective. Second, you have to
> waste an action or a master phase getting the intercept out.

Perhaps. But certain intercept cards go a long way. I don't think
it's bad to have one copy of KCRG and maybe one or two of London
Evening Star and/or Rumor Mill. They don't take up much room, if
they don't come up you do without but if they do, you suddenly have
the option to block stealth actions like votes and so forth. I think
this is clearly a case of a small amount of something going a long,
long way.

> Third, you then have to waste a minion _not_ rushing something to
> sit around waiting to block something.

The occasional Forced Awakening is not going to cost you any rushes.
It will occasionally take up hand space, which is bad. But the
ability to surprise your predator or prey with a combat they hadn't
expected will prevent them from playing their hand out with impunity.
It makes a difference. It sure as hell makes a difference to me
when I'm dealing with a combat deck and I see this happen. Again,
a small amount of something goes a long way (I'm not talking about
a lot of Wakes, only a sprinkling of them). It has a cost, but
relative to the benefit, it's well worth it in my experience.

> And very often, this leads to
> you beating up your predator instead of your prey, which is not always
> what you want.

Granted, reactions are less control than actions. But if you don't
want to beat someone up, don't use the Wake. It's an _option_. That's
important if you find your predator attempt to sensory dep your Beast,
Leatherface of Detroit.

Fred

You really have _zero_ room for intercept or untap. Trying to work in

>Ideally, you beat up all of your prey's vampires as soon as they get
>influenced out, before they ever get to take an action - and with your

This is backwards IMHO. Most good decks have a signifigant offensive
threat, and you need to blunt this proactively. Your predator is your
first target, unless he's playing some sort of defensive deck, when
you can thank him for helping you win. You have to walk a fine line
between keeping them from hurting you, and just setting him up for
your grandprey.

Your prey you want to actually let get started, so he can do some damage
to your grandprey for you, both setting him up for after you've ousted
your prey, and keeping him from getting to strong -- without the (yet)
having to rush cross table. Also if you torporize all of his vampires
right off the bat, he may well not influence out any more, figuring you
can't bleed for much. This can be frustrating.

At some point you'll have to go cross table as well, but that tends to
be obvious.

Obedience sucks, and there's not really much you can do about it.
Fortitude isn't nearly so threatening, and you can often blow through
it provided it isn't supported by agg damage or something similar.
In my experience maneuvers can be more of a pain in the ass than
fortitude.

My general problem with this is that any delay is always to the detriment
of the Rush deck. Rush, much more than other deck archetypes, relies
on speed of execution (in both senses) to win (in my limited experience --
see my plaintive posts on a different thread). There are precious few
actions that are critical enough that blocking them makes up for

case that I can think of where a Rush deck might want to block an
action, they'd be better off attacking the entities benefited by that
action -- vampires.

I couldn't figure out why you kept calling them "press"
locations, and then I just got it: because they're all news
media. Funny!

In my experience, most rush decks (though not all) rely on
small vampires to (a) keep their vamps from biting too deeply
into their starting pool, so that they have at least some
cushion to work with when people start damaging them, and (2)
make sure that they can get out vamps early in the game to
start making carnage. Because of that, skill cards show up
a lot (at least in my rush decks). In rush decks that use
fewer skill cards (and bigger vampires), there is usually
some other schtick being used - 2nd Traditions, 5ths, Minion
Taps, Anathemas, or some such; these are already generally
not pure rush decks and the wake/intercept angle is therefore
less of a divergence for them.

Also, the other piece of why I often find Wakes ineffective
in rush decks is that most opposing decks that want to do
bad things to me have already considered the possibility of
being blocked, and are either playing with stealth or other
means of getting their actions through, making it unlikely
that I'll be able to block even if I do wake. There are
exceptions of course - tap and bleed, etc - but even the
Sensory Deprivation that you cited as being at no stealth
can have +1 stealth added with Fata Morgana (fine if you have
out an intercept location already, but if not, you're just

Maybe so. I think it does depend on the metagame environment
you're looking at, as well as how intimidated your opponents
can be by seeing that you may have an occasional Wake and +1
intercept.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
>
> Frederick Scott wrote:
> >
> > James Hamblin wrote:
> > >
> > > Just because a card is flexible doesn't mean I want to play with it.
> >
> > No, but *I* do. And you asked why a person would have it. That's why.
> > The fact that *you* would choose not play with it is not per se a reason.
>
> The argument that I'm refuting is that "every deck should include this
> card".

Understood. Keep in mind that I concede that it depends on your metagame.

> > Anyway, to get back to the issue at hand, I'm saying that the fact that
> > it's OK with me that my opponents may choose to spend minion actions
> > depriving me of the votes on the card does *not* mean - as you erroneously
> > concluded - that "the card is ... marginal". It just gives them some
> > latitude about whether they want me to have the votes or spend their
> > minion actions. I assert that neither is a good choice for them; thus,
> > the card is a good card - even if I never get a single vote from it.
> > (In fact, the way it works, it's even *better* if I never get a single
> > vote from it than it is if I occasional do.)
>
> Let me put it this way. Let's say I have a Lasombra rush-combat deck.
> In theory, I could put in a couple Power Structures, since that's a good
> Lasombra vote card. But doing that will defocus the deck, and having the
> card will not directly help the deck win.

Well, actually, I might tend to use ONE Power Structure in such a deck. Just
me, I guess. Based on what I'm hearing from you and others, I'm just not
as impressed by what a single extra master card will do to combat deck
hand jam. (No reason to include two of them, certainly. That's another
straw man argument. No one was suggesting using two or more Powerbase:
Madrids in every deck, either.)

> > > _That's_ the point. There are many decks for which this card does
> > > nothing. I agree that every deck should have vote defense. But this
> > > ain't it, unless you're willing to try to protect it.
> >

> > I contradict. There are no decks for which this card does nothing. It

> > is either vote defense or it is something that my opponents must expend
> > minion actions on.
>
> No. _If_ it is vote defense,

Of course, it's vote defense.

> _then_ it _might_ be something your
> opponents expend actions on. And even if that becomes necessary, it
> probably won't be more than one action (assuming you're not defending
> it, which is where this all started) every three turns or so.

...and I think that's pretty good for an MPA and a pool. Period.

>
> > The risk in the card - aside from contesting and the
> > usual theivery/destruction risk that any location is subject to - is that
> > if I have no votes and my opponents have no votes and no bloodhunts/Elysium
> > destructions/etc. votes come up, *then* it is a useless card. This is
> > obviously only possible if I have no votes in my deck, so that's when it
> > behooves me to consider my metagame. But if political decks are popular
> > with my local crowd, it's still likely to be worthwhile.
>
> So you can't conceive of a metagame where you would (a) be playing a
> deck that does not vote and (b) not feel the need to play this card?

I can conceive of one, but that was never the question. I never said, "This
card is ALWAYS useful in ALL circumstances." Just that I can believe that
players may find it useful in all their decks - but it depends on the local
metagame. If this the source of our dispute - you're saying some metagames may
not call for this card in every deck and I'm saying that some metagames may -
then we can probably end the debate.

> > > But if they out-vote you anyway, you just wasted that pool and that MPA.
> >
> > OK, sure, if one guy gets a table lock that's five votes greater than the
> > rest of the field, it could be useless as well. That's seldom the case so
> > I'm not going to take that into account in my thinking. If that makes you
> > paranoid to think about, I guess our mileage does vary.
>
> You seem to be saying that this card is useful because it lets you stick
> your finger in the political pudding, regardless of whether it helps you
> win or defeat votes.

No. Please read what I wrote. I just got through saying, and I'll repeat,
vote locks that don't care about four vote permanent showing up are extremely
rare.

> > > > Perhaps. But certain intercept cards go a long way.
> > >
> > > ...toward letting you intercept things. Sure! But what if you don't
> > > want to do that? Then there's no use having the card.
> >
> > It's not so much that I want to that specifically. But it's very
> > very useful to slow down the development of both your predator and
> > prey's positions. And a little bit of stuff like this does have a
> > striking effect towards that end. I understand your desire to go
> > balls out as you do your rush combat. I'm just saying that if you
> > perhaps sacrifice the odd master phase action, pool, and occasionally
> > draw and hold a Forced Awakening, the amount of delay you reap from
> > it has always seemed to me to be well worth the minor inconvenience.
>
> To sacrifice an active combat for a passive combat that may or may not
> happen (modulo stealth) and may or may not be directed at the right
> vampire?

True. But I find stealthy decks to be uncommon enough that I don't have
to worry about whether it happens. And a few combats directed against the
"wrong vampire" aren't that bad a thing. And there are rather nice
advantages to weigh against this.

> > > But it costs yet more space in your deck, and yet more focus.
> >
> > Understood. This is a calculated risk.
>
> Rush decks without Wakes/Intercept already have a problem with hand jam
> and card flow. This would exacerbate the problem.

Agreed.

> > > You say this as if you think I haven't _tried_ having intercept and
> > > wakes in a combat deck. I have. It doesn't work.
> >
> > Well, as I said, it works for me. And when I play the other side of
> > it, it certainly slows me down when I see other combat decks do it.
>
> You're saying "it sure does suck when some combat monster blocks one of
> my stealthy actions, so it must be a good strategy". That's faulty
> logic. I could say "it sure did suck when I got ousted that one time by
> Screw the Masquerade!" but that doesn't make it a good card.

It is not faulty logic. What's faulty logic is your comparing these two
unlike statements, which is a total semantic straw man. When I say that
it sure sucks when an action gets blocked, it's because this actually
*definitately* hurts my game. Therefore it can be only good for my
opponent. When someone laments about getting ousted by being unable to
prevent the play of a marginal card, they would say such a thing due to
a sense of irony. If you can't discern the difference and why this is
a poor comparison, then we have little to discuss.

Fred
